summary: This standards-track memo describes how to carry a 64 kbit/s data channel unchanged inside RTP packets, using a pseudo-codec called Clearmode. It also registers the audio/clearmode media type. Clearmode is a basic feature of VoIP media gateways.

plainLanguage.summary: Some phone lines carry raw data rather than voice. This document says how to put that data in internet packets without changing it.

questions: what is clear channel data in voip
subtitle: How to carry a raw 64 kbit/s data channel untouched inside RTP packets, using a pseudo-codec called Clearmode.

tldr.problem: VoIP media gateways must carry data streams, such as ISDN data, that cannot go through voice coding and need a transparent relay, but RTP had no payload type for that.
tldr.mechanism: Clearmode is a pseudo-codec that does no encoding at all. It packs 8-bit samples taken at 8000 Hz, which is 64 kbit/s, into RTP packets, and it registers the audio/clearmode media type.
tldr.outcome: Gateways get a standard way to signal and relay clear-channel data, and it can share an SDP media line with codecs such as G.711.

today: RFC 4040 is a Proposed Standard. According to the unit metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated by any later RFC.

sections.title: Why Clearmode Exists
sections.content:
VoIP Media Gateways convert between analog or ISDN terminals and packet networks. They usually process the data, for example with echo cancellation, DTMF detection and especially coding and decoding. But some streams allow no processing beyond packetization. ISDN data terminals, for instance, produce streams that are not compatible with the non-linear encoding used for voice.

Those streams need a transparent real-time relay of 64 kbit/s data in RTP packets, often called clear-channel data or 64 kbit/s unrestricted. No encoder or decoder is needed, but a unique payload type and a MIME type for signaling are. Examples of current use are "ISDN 7 kHz voice" and "ISDN data". Any application that needs no special encoding can use it.
sections.plainLanguage: Voices get squashed to travel on the internet, but some data would be ruined by squashing. Clearmode lets that data travel exactly as it is.

sections.title: Packetizing the Data Stream
sections.content:
Clearmode does no encoding or decoding. It only packetizes. The data is sample oriented, with one octet (8 bits) per sample. A sample rate of 8000 Hz MUST be used, which works out to 64 kbit/s per channel.

There is no limit on samples per packet other than the 64 kbyte limit of IP. The number of samples SHOULD be less than the path MTU minus the combined packet header length, and it SHOULD be reduced further if tunnels or security encapsulation are expected.

Handling is similar to PCMU and PCMA in RFC 3551. Each octet SHALL be octet-aligned in the RTP packet, and the sign bit corresponds to the most significant bit of the octet.
sections.plainLanguage: The data is cut into little one-byte pieces, 8000 of them each second, and put into packets in order without changing a single piece.

sections.title: RTP Header Settings
sections.content:
The timestamp SHALL be set as described in RFC 3550. The marker bit is always zero, and silence suppression does not apply to Clearmode streams. The payload type is dynamically assigned and is not given in this document. Other RTP header fields are used as specified in RFC 3550 and any applicable profile.

The RFC specifies RTP over unicast and multicast UDP as well as TCP. That does not preclude other lower-layer protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has a label. For Clearmode the 'marker' flag is always off, and nobody skips the quiet parts, since data has no silence.

sections.title: The audio/clearmode Media Type
sections.content:
The document registers the MIME subtype audio/clearmode. There are no required parameters. The optional parameters are ptime, the length of time in milliseconds represented by the media in a packet, and maxptime, the maximum amount of media per packet in milliseconds. The type is defined only for transfer via RTP.

The audio top-level type was chosen because the dominant uses are expected to be telephony and voice gateway related. It lets Clearmode share the port in an SDP m= line with codecs such as G.711, which would not be possible otherwise. The intended usage is COMMON.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration gives Clearmode an official name tag so devices can say 'this call is Clearmode' when they set up a call.

sections.title: Mapping to SDP
sections.content:
The media type maps to SDP in the standard way. audio goes in the m= line as the media name, clearmode goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name, and ptime and maxptime go in a=ptime and a=maxptime.

The RFC's example uses audio/clearmode; ptime=10. Names are case-insensitive. Encoding names are commonly shown in upper case and MIME subtypes in lower case.
sections.plainLanguage: When two phones set up a call, they write 'Clearmode' on a form with a few details, like how much data goes in each packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Clearmode is subject to the security considerations of RFC 3550 and adds no security services of its own. Confidentiality comes from encryption, for example the Secure RTP profile (RFC 3711).

A receiver may be overloaded by too many packets. Network-layer authentication MAY be used to discard unwanted sources, though its processing cost may be too high. Overload can also happen if the sender uses a smaller packetization period than the receiver can handle, and ptime can be used to negotiate a suitable one.

RTP is in general not appropriate for reliable octet streams, and TCP is better then. Packet loss from congestion affects Clearmode as it does other payload formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Clearmode itself does not hide your data, so you lock it separately. Too many packets can swamp a receiver, so the two sides agree on packet size first.

data.title: Clearmode in SDP
data.code:
audio/clearmode; ptime=10

m=audio 12345 RTP/AVP 97
a=rtpmap:97 CLEARMODE/8000
a=ptime:10
